newsitem.title: UK: Lonrho profits up, works on split despite EU probe.
newsitem.headline: Lonrho profits up, works on split despite EU probe.

text.p: Conglomerate Lonrho Plc announced a 12.6 percent rise in full-year profits Thursday and said its break-up plan had not been derailed by a European Union investigation involving the company.
The widely diversified company said it remained committed to breaking up its mining and African trading business after the sale of the Princess hotel chain had been completed.

The EU recently began probing acquisition of a 28 percent stake in Lonrho by South African mining giant Anglo American. European Union officials have barred Anglo from voting its Lonrho shares pending their investigation into possible competition complications due to Anglo's interests in the platinum industry.
"It (the probe) won't stop me from going to shareholders and asking them for permission to do something in terms of a (split-up) or a sale," Lonrho Chief Executive Nick Morrell said.
Together with South African rival Gencor, Anglo and Lonrho control about 60 percent of world output of platinum, used in automotive exhaust catalysts.

Lonrho said it plans to stick to the precious metal operations after the EU earlier barred it from merging its platinum activities with Gencor's. The South African company is still fighting the decision.
"We intend to make our future as an independent company producing platinum. What that does to Anglo or Gencor is not Lonrho's issue," Morrell told Reuters in an interview.
Lonrho, with pre-tax profit before exceptional items rising to 170 million pounds ($285 million) from 151 million ($253 million) a year ago, first announced its break-up plans a year ago.
But after several delays and adjustments, the only step taken so far has been the October sale of its Metropole hotel chain to Britain's Stakis Plc.
Morrell said he hoped to conclude the Princess divestment and the ensuing slit-up as soon as possible, but declined to be more specific.

Lonrho's results for the year ended Sept. 30 were boosted by improved performances of its hotels, and its agricultural and other trading operations. But the profit rise, which was bigger than analysts had expected, was dampened by lower mining results, which were hit by falling mineral prices and devaluation of the rand, Lonrho said.
